contextPassage.title: Bearing Witness
contextPassage.text:
Few works of American literature have generated as much critical controversy, or as much durable enchantment, as those that attempt to render visible what the dominant culture has sought to make invisible. The literary tradition of bearing witness — of insisting on the dignity and complexity of lives that powerful forces have tried to subjugate, dismiss, or reduce to abstraction — is not merely an aesthetic endeavour. It is, at its crux, a political one. And it is one that demands of its practitioners both consummate skill and extraordinary candor.

To read the great protest narratives of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries is to confront, again and again, a central dilemma: how does a writer convey the reality of abject suffering without reducing those who suffer to the status of objects for the reader's pity? The temptation to produce a depiction so harrowing that it overwhelms the reader's critical faculties is real. So too is the opposite temptation — to aestheticise misery until it becomes palatable, to trade the unwieldy truth for something more readily absorbed. Neither approach, most critics would concede, produces literature that endures.

What does endure is work that refuses this false choice. In the most powerful examples of the genre — whether we think of the slave narratives promulgated in the antebellum United States, the testimonies of emigrants who sought to retain their identities in hostile new environments, or the fiction of writers working under authoritarian regimes — what is most striking is not sentiment but precision. These writers did not merely aspire to move their audiences. They sought to ascertain the truth of their circumstances and to articulate it with the directness of people who had no patience for the trifling comforts of evasion.

The challenge, of course, is not only literary. It is historical. The documents that survive, the archives that have been preserved, the accounts that have been deemed worthy of record — all of these bear the imprint of the prejudices of those who controlled the means of preservation. Prominent voices were retained; others were relegated to silence. The recollections of the powerful were substantiated by institutional records; the recollections of the dispossessed were treated as mere anecdote. This asymmetry is not incidental to the problem of writing history. It is the problem.

Contemporary scholars attempting to corroborate oral traditions with written records frequently encounter a labyrinthine tangle of incomplete sources, each shaped by the ideological commitments of those who created them. What appears to be abundant evidence on one side of a historical question often reflects nothing more than the diligence with which one group preserved its version of events. The scatterbrained impression that history gives of certain communities is not a reflection of their lives but of whose lives were considered worth recording.

This is why the question of how we construe literary evidence is so onerous — and so important. A novel is not a census, but it is not nothing, either. When a writer of the stature of Frederick Douglass or Harriet Jacobs expends extraordinary care in the construction of a narrative, that care is itself a form of testimony. The tentative, circumspect tone that occasionally surfaces in such texts is not weakness; it is an acknowledgement of the stakes — an awareness that to overstate is to invite dismissal, and that the dominant culture will seize upon any imprecision as grounds for extending its indifference.

The most dangerous form of reading, in this context, is the superficial one — the reading that evokes sympathy without generating understanding, that is moved by suffering without being troubled by its causes. Such reading is consoling, which is precisely why it should be viewed with scorn. The enduring works in this tradition do not console. They impose discomfort. They stimulate rather than soothe. They invite, and sometimes compel, a recollection of things that conventional culture would prefer to abate — a remembrance not of the past as it has been curated, but of the past as it was experienced by those who were given no say in the curation.

To read in this way is strenuous and, at times, irate-making. It is also, for those willing to sustain the effort, among the most consequential things that literature can do. The yearn it produces is not for a vanished world but for a more honest engagement with the one we inhabit — a world in which the aggregate of human experience, in all its diversity and inequity, is at last allowed to be seen as distinct, irreducible, and worthy of deference.
